latin: Canga, marsupiālis fēmina, māter Ruī, in marsūpiō<sup>1</sup> Porcellum prō Ruō sēcum ferēns*. — Age! venī, Rue cārissime. Cubandī tempus est. — Porcellum<sup>2</sup> ē marsūpiō trahit.
Porcellus. — Ēheu!
Can., ēvidenter nōn intellēxit quid Porcellī querimōnia<sup>3</sup> significāret. — Imprīmīs balneum!
Por. — Ēheu! — Sociōs timidē oculīs quaerit, sed cēterī absunt*.
Can. — Anceps haereō<sup>4</sup> et dubitō an sapiēns prōpositum nōn sit, balneō hodiē frīgidō ūtī. Amāsne balnea frīgida, Rue cārissime?
Por., quī nunquam fuerat amātor balneōrum, graviter anhēlāns horret<sup>5</sup>. — Canga, intellegō tempus īnstāre sincērā fide<sup>6</sup> loquendī.
Magna vōce. — Nōn sum Ruus, Porcellus sum!
Can. — Ita est, corculum<sup>7</sup> meum, ita; etiam vōcem Porcellī imitārīs. — Sāpōnem permagnum ex armāriō sūmit.
Por. — Nōnne vidēs? Num cālīgās<sup>8</sup>? Adspice!
Can. — Videō tē, Rue cārissime. Et scīs quod tibi dē sannīs<sup>9</sup> dīxī:
«Porcellum imitāns, adultus<sup>10</sup> porcellus vidēberis; et mente finge quantum id tē pigēre*<sup>11</sup> possit*».
Age! In balneum! Cave nē idem saepius<sup>12</sup> iterum dīcam.
Antequam quid fīat* intellegat, Porcellus in balneō est. Cangā eum pannō<sup>13</sup> crassō<sup>14</sup> et sāpōnātō et quasi lōreō vehementer fricat.
Por. — Ai! Sine mē abīre*! Porcellus sum!
Can. — Nōlī* os<sup>15</sup> aperīre, cārissime, aut sāpō intrābit. Ecce! Quod erat dēmōnstrandum<sup>16</sup>!
latinAccented: Canga, marsupiā́lis fḗmina, māter Ruī, in marsū́piō<sup>1</sup> Porcéllum prō Ruō sēcum ferēns*. — Age! venī, Rue cāríssime. Cubándī tempus est. — Porcéllum<sup>2</sup> ē marsū́piō trahit.
Porcéllus. — Ḗheu!
Can., ēvidénter nōn intellḗxit quid Porcéllī querimṓnia<sup>3</sup> significā́ret. — Imprī́mīs bálneum!
Por. — Ḗheu! — Sóciōs tímidē óculīs quaerit, sed cḗterī absunt*.
Can. — Anceps háereō<sup>4</sup> et dúbitō an sápiēns prōpósitum nōn sit, bálneō hódiē frī́gidō ūtī. Amā́sne bálnea frī́gida, Rue cāríssime?
Por., quī nunquam fúerat amā́tor balneṓrum, gráviter anhḗlāns horret<sup>5</sup>. — Canga, intéllegō tempus īnstā́re sincḗrā fide<sup>6</sup> loquéndī.
Magna vōce. — Nōn sum Ruus, Porcéllus sum!
Can. — Ita est, córculum<sup>7</sup> meum, ita; étiam vōcem Porcéllī imitā́rīs. — Sāpṓnem permágnum ex armā́riō sūmit.
Por. — Nōnne vidēs? Num cālī́gās<sup>8</sup>? Ádspice!
Can. — Vídeō tē, Rue cāríssime. Et scīs quod tibi dē sannīs<sup>9</sup> dīxī:
«Porcéllum ímitāns, adúltus<sup>10</sup> porcéllus vidḗberis; et mente finge quantum id tē pigḗre*<sup>11</sup> possit*».
Age! In bálneum! Cave nē idem sáepius<sup>12</sup> íterum dīcam.
Ántequam quid fīat* intéllegat, Porcéllus in bálneō est. Cangā eum pannō<sup>13</sup> crassō<sup>14</sup> et sāpōnā́tō et quasi lṓreō veheménter fricat.
Por. — Ai! Sine mē abī́re*! Porcéllus sum!
Can. — Nōlī* os<sup>15</sup> aperī́re, cāríssime, aut sāpō intrā́bit. Ecce! Quod erat dēmōnstrándum<sup>16</sup>!
english: Kanga, female kangaroo, mother of Roo, carrying with her in her pouch Piglet instead of Roo. — Come on! Come, Roo my darling. It is time [to go] to sleep. — She takes Piglet out of her pouch.
Piglet. — Ouch!
Kanga, evidently she did not understand what P.-'s complaint meant. — First the bath!
P. — Ouch! — He looks timidly with his eyes for his companions, but the others are not there.
Kanga. — I remain undecided and I wonder whether it would not be a [good] (wise) [idea] (plan) to take a cold bath today. Do you like cold baths, Roo my darling?

P.-, who had never been a lover of baths, [his breath frightfully cut short] (heavily panting shudders). — Kanga, I understand that the time presses [to tell you the truth] (by sincere good faith to speak).
[Very loudly] (by great voice). — I'm not Roo, I'm Piglet!
Kanga. — Yes, my little heart, yes. You even imitate Piglet's voice. — She takes from the cupboard a gigantic soap.
P. — Can't you see? Have you [got your eyes shut] (N. 8)? Look!
Kanga. — I see you, Roo my darling. And you know what I told you on the subject of faces:
«By imitating Piglet, [when you are grown up] (become adult little pig you will seem) you will look like a piglet; and (in spirit) [imagine] how much that could disgust you».
Come on! In the bath! Be careful that I don't have to repeat (again to say) the same thing too often.
Before he understands [what is happening] (what is done), Piglet is in the bath. Kanga rubs him [vigorously] (vehemently) with a thick [towel] (piece of cloth), full of soap and hard as leather.
P. — Ouch! Let me go! I'm Piglet!
Kanga. — Don't open your mouth, my darling, or [you'll swallow] some soap (will enter). There! That's what had to be demonstrated!

footnotes: Marsupium, -ii, n., the pocket, whence marsupiales, marsupials, animals that have a pouch (kangaroo, opossum, etc.).
Porcellus, -i, m.; diminutive of porcus, -i, m., itself a synonym of sus, suis, m. (see L. 58, N. 3).
Querimonia, -ae, f., derived from queror, -eris, -i, questus sum, to complain, which must not be confused with quaerere, to seek, which you will see again in phrase 4.

Haereo, -es, -ere, haesi, haesum, lit. to be attached (to adhere). — Anceps, ancipitis, adj., which we have already seen (L. 31, P. 4) in the sense of doubtful thing, refers here to a person who doubts.

Horreo, -es, -ere, -ui, v.i. to bristle, to shiver, to be afraid; one also says: horresco, -es, -ere, horrui; the series of the perfectum being the same for the two verbs. Horresco referens*, I shudder [in] telling (this story).
Fides, -ei, f., faith, belief, good faith; from fido, -is, -ere, fisus sum, semi-deponent verb (+ dat.), to trust in.
Corculum, -i, n., diminutive of cor, cordis, n., the heart.
Caligare, to be in the fog, in the dark; caligo, -inis, f., thick smoke, obscurity, fog. Not to be confused with caliga, -ae, f., the boot (short i, since it is not accented).

Adultus, -a, -um, become big, perfect passive participle of adolesco, -is, -ere, adolevi, adultum, to grow up; while the present participle adulescens means: in the course of becoming big (that is to say young man).

Piget* (me, te, etc.) impersonal verb, to be repugnant (lit. it disgusts me, you, etc., it is repugnant to me). Likewise paenitet* me, I repent of, and pudet* me, I am ashamed of. These impersonal verbs can however have a subject if it is in the THIRD person, here: id.
Saepius: comparative of saepe, adv., often. What would be the superlative of this adverb? — Answer: saepissime. Note that these three adverbial forms do not correspond to adjectives.

Loreus, -a, -um, of leather; lorum, -i, n., strap. Lorica, -ae, f., cuirass. Currus loricatus, an armoured chariot, a tank. In spite of appearances, the kinship between the first two words and the last two is doubtful.
Os, oris, n., the mouth, the face; the rest of the sentence clearly shows that it is not os, ossis, the bone.
Abbreviated Q.E.D., which corresponds to our Q.E.D.
comments: Esca, -ae, f., food, and esculentus, -a, -um, are of the same family as edere (L. 40, N. 4). — Gausapa, -ae, f., designates a coarse or plush fabric. — Mitis, -e, gentle (in character); dulcis, gentle to taste; mollis, gentle to touch. — Physica, -ae, f., has a broader sense than our present-day Physics and designates everything relating to nature (in Greek physis), that is to say also Physics as well as Natural History. — Animus, -i, m., mind, heart, courage, the whole of the intellectual and moral functions of man. Anima, -ae, f., has in principle a more restricted sense: the breath of life, which the animal also has (animal, -alis, n.). But it is used in the senses of breath, life and, by extension, soul.

latin: Quō it villicus? — Porcīs ēscam affert*.
Ovēs et vaccae in prātīs vagantur.
Ubicumque herbam esculentam inveniunt, ibīdem pāscendī causā manent.
Quis est ille Puus vel Pū?
Ursus puerī Christophorī est.
Quid! Potestne* puerulus ursum habēre?
Ursī sunt saevissima animālia.
Ita! Ursī ferī sunt saevissimī, ursī ē gausapā autem mītissimī.
Animal ē gausapā animal vērum nōn est: animā eī deest*.
Tālia dīcunt physicī; auctōrēs autem quī ad puerōrum dēlectātiōnem scrībunt aliter sentiunt.
In librīs ad ūsum puerōrum, tam animālibus vērīs quam animālibus commentīciīs nōn sōlum animus, sed etiam hūmānī sunt mōrēs.
Nōlī manūs in marsūpiīs tenēre!
latinAccented: Quō it víllicus? — Porcīs ēscam affert*.
Ovēs et vaccae in prātīs vagántur.
Ubicúmque herbam esculéntam invéniunt, ibī́dem pāscéndī causā manent.
Quis est ille Puus vel Pū?
Ursus púerī Christóphorī est.
Quid! Potéstne* puérulus ursum habḗre?
Ursī sunt saevíssima animā́lia.
Ita! Ursī ferī sunt saevíssimī, ursī ē gáusapā autem mītíssimī.
Ánimal ē gáusapā ánimal vērum nōn est: ánimā eī deest*.
Tā́lia dīcunt phýsicī; auctṓrēs autem quī ad puerṓrum dēlectātiṓnem scrībunt áliter séntiunt.
In librīs ad ūsum puerṓrum, tam animā́libus vērīs quam animā́libus commentī́ciīs nōn sōlum ánimus, sed étiam hūmā́nī sunt mōrēs.
Nōlī manūs in marsū́piīs tenḗre!
english: Where is the farmer going? — He is bringing food to the pigs.
The ewes and the cows wander in the meadows.
[Wherever] they find [good] (edible) grass, [there] they stay [to graze] (by reason of grazing).
Who is this Pooh or Pu?
It's the bear of [little] Christopher.
What! [Can a little boy have] a bear?
Bears are very ferocious animals.
Yes, wild bears are very ferocious, but plush bears are very gentle.
A plush animal is not a real animal: it lacks the [breath of] life.
[That is what] (such things) the naturalists say; but [the] authors who write [for the amusement of] (to the delectation of) children [are of another opinion] (differently feel).
In children's books, [the] real animals as well as [the] imaginary animals [have] not only a soul, but still human [ways] (customs) of living.
Don't keep your hands in your pockets!
